{{Short description|Italian mathematician (1895–1975)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2026}}
{{Infobox scientist|occupation=teacher and mathematician|education =University of Pisa|field=[[Classical mechanics|rational mechanics]]|image = Photo of Maria Pastori.jpg}}
'''Maria Pastori''' (10 March 1895 - 17 April 1975) was an Italian mathematician and teacher. She was a Professor of [[Classical mechanics|Rational Mechanics]] at the [[University of Milan]], and worked on [[differential calculus]] and the application of mathematics to [[Electromagnet|electromagnets]].

== Early life and education ==
Pastori was born in [[Milan]] on 10 March 1895, to a family of eight children.<ref name="l-z dictionary" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Udeschini |first=Paolo |date=1975-12-01 |title=Maria Pastori |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02925595 |journal=Rendiconti del Seminario Matematico e Fisico di Milano |language=it |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=19–28 |doi=10.1007/BF02925595 |issn=1424-9294|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The family was of limited means and could not afford education for the children beyond what was provided by the public school system. Pastori excelled in mathematics, which was encouraged by one of her teachers, who aided her in getting a scholarship to Maria Agnesi School, a [[magisterial school]] (similar to a teacher's college).<ref name="l-z dictionary">{{cite book|last1=Ogilvie|first1=Harvey|last2=Marilyn Bailey|first2=Joy Dorothy|author-link=Marilyn Bailey Ogilvie|author2-link=Joy Harvey|title=The Biographical Dictionary of Women in Science: L-Z|isbn=0415920388|pages=987|year=2000|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/biographicaldict00ogil_0}}</ref><ref name="nature and growth">{{cite book|last1=Kramer|first1=Edna E.|title=The Nature and Growth of Modern Mathematics|date=1970|isbn=0-691-08305-3|page=706|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LLEZQC74gVcC&q=The+Nature+and+Growth+of+Modern+Mathematics}}</ref> 

After completing her studies at the magisterial school, Pastori then went on to teach elementary school near Milan. While teaching, Pastori studied further with her sister [[Giuseppina Pastori|Giuseppina]] (who became a physician and biologist).<ref name="nature and growth" /><ref name="l-z dictionary" /> At the age of twenty, Pastori sat for the state exams and earned a baccalaureate with highest honours.<ref name="l-z dictionary" /> She earned a scholarship to the [[University of Pisa]] where she earned a doctorate, studying under geometer [[Luigi Bianchi]].<ref name="l-z dictionary" /> She earned laureate status on her dissertation. She supported herself during her studies by tutoring.<ref name="l-z dictionary" />

== Career ==
After earning her doctorate, Pastori became an assistant professor at the [[University of Milan]], working her way up to professor, and eventually becoming the chair of the [[Classical mechanics|rational mechanics]] department. Most of Pastori's research and publications were focused on extending differential calculus as developed by [[Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro]], as well as the application of mathematics to electromagnets.<ref name="l-z dictionary" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Osen |first=Lynn M. |url=https://archive.org/details/womeninmathemati00osen/mode/2up?q=Pastori |title=Women in mathematics |date=1974 |publisher=Cambridge, Mass., MIT Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-262-15014-9}}</ref> 

Pastori was made an extraordinary professor in 1965, and in 1971 [[Emeritus|professor emerita]].<ref name="l-z dictionary" />

She died on 17 April 1975 in Milan.<ref name="l-z dictionary" />
